newsitem.title: DUBAI: Smuggling of Iraqi diesel widespread in Gulf.
newsitem.headline: Smuggling of Iraqi diesel widespread in Gulf.

text.p: Illicit smuggling of Iraqi diesel oil has become widespread in the Gulf with a market created by local and international shipping firms eager to buy cheap fuel to power their vessels, Gulf shipping sources said on Wednesday.

As Iraqi and United Nations officials continue to discuss the next stage of an oil-for-food deal, Iraqi middlemen, foreign traders and shippers are doing a brisk and lucrative business that runs into hundreds of millions of dollars.

Although this trade has been rumbling on since U.N. sanctions were slapped on Iraq after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, shippers said that activity had stepped up since the end of last year because of high diesel prices in the international market.

"The price of Iraqi diesel is $30 to $50 a tonne below the international market price and when you want 4,000 tonnes or 5,000 tonnes for your ships it is very attractive," said one Gulf-based shipping executive who admitted to regularly buying Iraqi diesel and wanted to remain anonymous.

Though authorities across the Gulf have caught and impounded vessels involved in the smuggling, shippers said the number of arrests accounted for only a small part of the trade which is carried out on a cash and also barter basis.

Loaded at Iraq's southern ports with false or no paperwork, embargoed diesel is shipped to customers in barges and small vessels which cling to the shallow coastal waters of the Gulf to avoid capture by a U.S.-led multinational naval interception force mandated to implement sanctions against Iraq.
The diesel is then transfered out as sea to the paying ship owner with rare interference from authorities, shippers said.
Diesel is used by shipowners to run auxiliary and emergency power systems to back up main engines which run on fuel oil.
"It's going on throughout the Gulf but mainly centred in Fujairah and close to Iran," another source said.
Fujairah, a tiny emirate perched near the strategic Strait of Hormuz and one of the seven sheikhdoms that make up major oil-producer United Arab Emirates, is the Gulf's leading ship fueling centre.

Its coastline is dotted with a flotilla of foreign-flagged vessels ranging from giant supertankers to tug boats taking on fuel oil and marine diesel before heading on to load crude from the Gulf's oil powerhouses Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iran.
"That's a willing and waiting market," said a shipper.
U.S. officials at the U.N. last year presented documents alleging that contraband Iraqi gas oil was being transported through Iranian waters in violation of sanctions.
Iraq has denied breaking the embargo.

Another UAE emirate that has also attracted Iraqi diesel business is Sharjah which earlier this month felt the impact from a barge that ran aground and spilled more than 2,500 tonnes of diesel which was widely suspected to have come from Iraq.
Iraq is expected to resume crude exports under the U.N. oil-for-deal in August after Baghdad and the U.N. agree on an aid distribution plan.
